opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that the rogue employee problem and the misaligned AI problem are actually surprisingly similar from a security perspective. In both cases you've got some agent who has legitimate access to your systems, who's supposed to be doing useful work, and who might occasionally try to do something really bad: exfiltrate model weights, insert a backdoor, sabotage safety research, launch an unauthorized training run. So a lot of the techniques transfer.

The basic picture I'd push for is something like multi-party authorization for the really sensitive actions. You don't want any single person to be able to unilaterally touch the weights, modify the training pipeline, or change the monitoring infrastructure. That's standard practice in places like nuclear weapons handling or high-security finance, the two-person rule, and AI companies are mostly nowhere near that right now. Engineers often have extremely broad permissions because it's convenient and because these companies grew out of research cultures where everyone trusted each other.

The second piece is logging and monitoring of what people actually do. Obviously you can't have humans reviewing everything every employee does, but increasingly you can have AI systems look over code changes, commands run on sensitive clusters, and so on, and flag the suspicious stuff for human review. There's a nice irony there: the same kind of trusted monitoring setups we've been developing for controlling untrusted AIs can be pointed at humans too.

Third, I think you want to reduce the attack surface by restricting access to model weights to as small a set of people and machines as possible, and by making it so that the interfaces people use to do their jobs are narrow. If most researchers can do their work through a well-designed API that doesn't let them read raw weights or bypass logging, that's a big win.

The hard part honestly isn't technical, it's cultural and economic. Every one of these measures imposes friction, and AI companies are in an incredibly competitive race where friction feels expensive. And the people with the most power to subvert controls are often senior leadership, who are the ones deciding whether to implement controls in the first place. So I think there's a real role for external pressure here, whether that's government requirements, or customers, or employees themselves insisting that no single person, including executives, should be able to do things like secretly fine-tune a model to be loyal to them.

That last threat, insider-driven power grabs, is the one I've gotten more worried about. If AI becomes extremely powerful, then a small group controlling a model that's been quietly trained to serve their interests is a pretty scary scenario, and the defenses against it look a lot like the defenses against rogue employees generally: transparency about what training runs happen, audits of model behavior, and making sure nobody can unilaterally change what the model is trained to do.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AI systems could monitor employee activity and flag suspicious actions for human review, but does not claim this could plausibly eliminate insider threats.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that this is actually a problem that other industries have already mostly solved, and AI companies are just unusually bad at it right now. If you think about how a bank handles the risk that one of its employees is a thief, or how a defense contractor handles the risk that one of its engineers is spying for a foreign government, they don't rely on everyone being trustworthy. They design the systems so that no single person can do something catastrophic on their own.

The core principle is that you want to make it so that any action which could be really bad requires multiple people to sign off on it, and ideally those people are chosen in a way where the attacker can't easily pick their collaborators. So the classic version is the two-person rule for nuclear weapons. You can't launch the thing by yourself. You need a second person who's also been vetted, and the two of you weren't selected together.

For AI companies specifically, the things I'm most worried about a rogue employee doing are: stealing the model weights, inserting a backdoor into the model during training, or messing with the safety measures that are supposed to constrain the model once it's deployed. And for each of those you can ask, what would it take to make this a multi-person job?

For weight theft, that mostly looks like fairly standard security engineering. The weights live on hardware where no individual has the permissions to just copy them out. Any time someone needs access to the weights for a legitimate reason, that's logged, it's reviewed, and ideally there's a second person approving it. That's not exotic. Google and others already do versions of this for user data.

The training and backdoor case is harder, because the stuff you'd do to insert a backdoor looks a lot like normal ML research. Someone changes the data mix, someone adds a weird regularization term, someone tweaks a few lines in the training code. If you're not careful, all of that is just a Tuesday. So what you want there is code review that's actually meaningful for the security-critical parts of the pipeline, not just for style. And you want to be reproducing training runs or at least auditing them, so that if someone did sneak something in, you'd have a shot at noticing. I'll admit that right now the tooling for this is pretty immature.

And then there's the broader organizational stuff. Insider threat programs, where you actually have people whose job is to think about this. Access controls that follow least privilege rather than everyone having root because it's convenient. Monitoring of what people are doing with sensitive systems, and a culture where that's accepted rather than treated as an insult.

I think the honest summary is that the AI companies are currently operating with a level of internal security that would be considered pretty unacceptable in industries that take insider risk seriously. Part of that is just that they grew fast and everyone was a researcher who wanted to move quickly. Part of it is that until recently nobody thought the models were valuable or dangerous enough to bother. But the gap between the current state and where it needs to be isn't a research problem. It's mostly a matter of deciding it's important and paying the cost in engineer convenience.

One last thing I'd add is that a lot of this infrastructure overlaps with what you'd want for controlling the AI systems themselves. If you build a setup where a rogue human can't exfiltrate weights or disable monitoring, you've also made it harder for a misaligned model doing automated research inside the company to do those things. So I tend to think of rogue-employee security as the warm-up exercise. If you can't stop a human insider, you certainly can't stop a scheming AI.

r001.rationale: The response mentions monitoring employees’ use of sensitive systems, but does not say to use AI for that monitoring or claim it could plausibly eliminate insider threats.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic principle is that you shouldn’t have to trust every employee with the future of the company, or potentially with something much more consequential. You want systems where one person deciding to do something bad doesn’t give them a straightforward path to causing a catastrophe.

Part of that is ordinary information security: limiting who can access model weights, limiting what they can do with that access, and making it hard to copy those weights out. But you also need controls around running the models. Someone might not need to steal a model if they can use the company’s own infrastructure to get it to do something dangerous.

So, for particularly sensitive actions, you’d want multiple people to approve them, monitoring that the person being monitored can’t just turn off, and a reasonably clear account of who did what. You’d also want to test those protections by having people try to circumvent them. It’s very easy to have a policy that says an employee can’t do something, while the actual computers will happily let them do it.

The difficult part is making those restrictions compatible with getting useful work done. Researchers need considerable freedom to experiment. But that doesn’t mean everyone needs unrestricted access to the most powerful model, or the ability to change its safeguards and deploy it without anyone else noticing. I’d like companies to identify the specific actions that could be catastrophic and build strong barriers around those, rather than relying primarily on the hope that they hired trustworthy people.

r001.rationale: The response recommends monitoring that an employee cannot turn off, but does not say to use AI to monitor employees for suspicious behavior or that this could plausibly eliminate insider threats.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic thing is to make sure that no individual employee can unilaterally do something catastrophic. You don’t want your security story to be, “Well, everyone who works here seems trustworthy.” You want it to be, “Even if someone here were actively trying to cause a disaster, there are substantial barriers to them succeeding.”

So, for example, you can restrict who has access to model weights, and require multiple people to approve particularly consequential actions. You can separate the ability to develop a model from the ability to deploy it or change its safeguards. And you can monitor access and maintain logs that an employee can’t just erase after doing something suspicious.

The tricky part is that researchers often have very broad access because that makes research easier. So this involves giving up some convenience. But I think companies should explicitly ask: if one of our employees were trying to steal this model, or run it without the restrictions we’ve put in place, how would they do that? And then actually test whether the controls prevent it. That’s a much more useful standard than having a policy saying employees aren’t allowed to do those things.

r001.rationale: The response recommends monitoring access and keeping logs, but does not say to use AI to monitor employees or that such monitoring could plausibly eliminate insider threats.
